title: Service resilience rebuild notice and customer QA
audience: All enterprise and self-serve customers potentially affected by degraded generation or longer-than-usual latencies during the incident window on 2027-01-14 to 2027-01-15.
one_line_summary: We rebuilt a degraded GPU serving pool which temporarily affected some model generations; traffic is restored and we are providing validation steps and optional replay choices for customers.
statuspage_update: Summary: We have completed a staged rebuild of the affected inference pool and returned traffic to normal routing. Impact window: 2027-01-14 22:40 UTC to 2027-01-15 05:20 UTC. Customers may have observed elevated latency and occasional truncated or inconsistent responses during this period. Current status: Resolved for all regions; services are operating within SLOs. Next update: Final customer-facing postmortem to be published within 7 business days.
customer_postmortem: Background: During routine autoscaling and kernel refresh activity on the GPU serving layer, a subset of worker instances failed to restore their KV caches and prefix caches correctly after a rolling reboot. This led to prolonged cold starts for some requests and, in a small number of cases, partially truncated structured outputs for long-running streams. What we did: - Isolated the affected pool and halted further automated rollouts. - Performed a staged rebuild of the node image with revised cache initialization flags. - Re-routed customer traffic to healthy pools while we validated behavior under load. - Executed targeted replays for enterprise customers who requested assistance and offered guided verification steps. Root cause (high level): A recent kernel optimization changed the startup ordering for the KV cache population process. Under a specific timing window when workers restarted at scale, the cache population completed after the first request batches were processed, causing requests to observe empty or partially-populated caches. This manifested as higher latency and occasional missing tokens in structured responses. Corrective actions taken: - Reverted the startup ordering change and deployed a fix to ensure cache warm-up before accepting traffic. - Added a startup-probe that prevents a worker from being marked healthy until KV/prefix caches reach a minimal warm state. - Expanded unit and integration tests to simulate large-scale rolling restarts and verify cache population invariants. - Updated runbooks to include an explicit staged rollback threshold and automated traffic drainer to protect in-flight requests. Customer-facing remediation and verification guidance: - Immediate check: For customers who saw truncated or inconsistent outputs, re-run a representative prompt against the same model and model-version over the next 24–72 hours and compare outputs. If you see consistent differences that affect correctness, contact support with sample request IDs. - Replay option: Enterprise customers who opted in can request a guided replay of affected requests where we preserved request payloads and logs. Replays are performed only with customer consent and an agreed time window. - Model pin suggestion: To prevent any surprise changes during our ongoing optimizations, customers may pin to an explicit model-version in their Redwood configuration until you choose to unpin. How we validated resolution: - Smoke tests across region pools at spike and sustained QPS. - Determinism checks for structured-output tasks (length, tokenization parity) run on a prompt corpus representative of customer workloads. - Cross-region consistency checks for embeddings and reranks. Observations post-fix: Error rates and tail latencies returned to baseline within 45 minutes of traffic reroute; no new cases of truncated structured streams observed in the last 72 hours. Service credit / compensation: Customers who experienced confirmed data-impacting truncations are eligible for a partial uptime credit or a replay service (technical assistance to reprocess requests). Please contact your account rep or support@redwood.ai to start a claim. Contact & escalation: - Primary support: support@redwood.ai (include sample request IDs and timestamps) - Enterprise success: asha.mehta@redwood.ai - Escalation: open Jira INFR-4567 with the subject line 'Replay/credit request - rebuilding incident' and tag your account. Timeline (UTC):

2027-01-14 23:05 — Spike in 99th percentile latency and increase in truncated structured responses reported by monitoring.
2027-01-14 23:22 — SREs flagged unusual cache warm-up timing and scoped to a single pool.
2027-01-14 23:50 — Decided to halt automated rollouts; initiated traffic reroute to healthy pools.

impact_summary: Scope: ~0.7% of customer requests in the affected time window saw elevated tail latency; ~0.02% of requests (across affected tenants) experienced structured-output truncation likely to change correctness for some use-cases. Regions: primarily US-west and EU-west pools during rolling activity. Models: impact observed across multiple model families using KV/prefix caching (generation and streaming endpoints).
root_cause_analysis: A kernel optimization inadvertently altered startup sequencing: the worker became healthy and accepted traffic before required cache population completed. Under scale, the first request batches raced ahead of cache warm-up. This produced cold-cache path behavior that increased latency and, in some streaming flows, resulted in truncated outputs. The change passed unit tests but lacked an integration test for large-scale rolling restarts and cache warm-up invariants.
preventative_measures: 1) Restore safe startup ordering and enforce cache warm-up gates. 2) Add startup-probe and health gating to platform orchestration. 3) Add distributed chaos/integration tests that simulate mass rolling restarts. 4) Add monitoring for cache-hit rates during restarts and automated circuit-breaker if hit rate falls below threshold. 5) Update release checklist to require an explicit restart-smoothness sign-off for kernel-level changes.
customer_validation_steps: 1) Select 3–5 representative prompts that exercise streaming/structured output in your integration. 2) Run them against the same model-version you used during the incident and capture outputs. 3) Compare token counts and key fields; if discrepancies appear, copy request IDs and samples into a support ticket. 4) If you want Redwood to run replays, include a list of request IDs and consent to replay in your ticket. 5) If you rely on deterministic embeddings or reranks, run a small sample corpus check (we recommend 50–200 items) and share hashes if you need assistance.
recommended_customer_actions:
- Pin critical routes to a model-version for the next 2 weeks if you prefer to avoid implicit runtime optimizations.
- Subscribe to our statuspage incident feed for real-time updates.
- Keep a short prompt test-suite in staging to detect regressions earlier; we can share a lightweight checklist.
- For high-sensitivity workloads, ask your customer success rep about assisted canarying on Dedicated pools.
faq:
Q: Will my data have been exposed during the incident?
A: No — this incident did not involve data plane leaks or unauthorized access. It was a compute/runtime ordering issue.

Q: How long will verification take?
A: Most checks (latency and determinism) complete within hours; if you request a replay or manual verification from Redwood our team will coordinate timelines per account and size of the request set.

Q: Can I get a list of affected request IDs?
A: We will provide preserved request logs for enterprise customers where we have consent to replay; for self-serve customers we provide guidance to identify suspicious request IDs in your own logs using timestamps and request hashes.
closing_note: We are sorry for the disruption. Our engineering and SRE teams prioritize reliability; the fix addresses the root cause and adds additional safeguards to prevent recurrence. We will follow up with a finalized postmortem and publish the integration test artifacts created as part of this remediation in an internal repo (link will be shared).
